title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
1 Introduction
A model edit that changes one behaviour usually changes others too. Model-editing work evaluates locality: inputs outside an edit’s scope should keep their predictions (Yao et al. 2023, sec. 2). ROME, for example, scores an edited fact by whether the model retains facts about nearby subjects (Meng et al. 2022, sec. 3.3). For a language edit, a demanding test is a related language. Zeroing parameters important for Spanish also raises Italian and Portuguese perplexity (Zhang et al. 2024, Table 11), and deactivating French neurons affects Spanish (Tang et al. 2024, sec. 3.3.1).
Parameter decompositions may allow narrower edits. adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) approximates each weight matrix by a sum of rank-one subcomponents, trained so that few are needed on any input (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 2). It follows earlier attribution-based and stochastic decompositions (Braun et al. 2025; Bushnaq et al. 2025). If a subcomponent is specific to one language, changing its scalar coefficient might alter that language while sparing its relatives.1
Bushnaq tested this possibility by training scalar coefficients of selected VPD subcomponents to suppress German (Bushnaq 2026). One subcomponent, chosen by its interpretation label, reached chance-level German with little English damage and spared French and Spanish, although it also damaged Italian.
Here I extend that test to three pairs of related languages: German (de)–Dutch (nl), Spanish (es)–Portuguese (pt) and French (fr)–Italian (it). In each pair, the first language is the target of deliberate damage and the second measures selectivity. A fixed numerical rule selects one subcomponent from target and English text. I compare its edits with rank-one LoRA, full-matrix fine-tuning and neuron edits. The related language in each pair (labelled protected in tables and figures) is excluded from the selection and training inputs in this comparison.
An edit could appear more selective simply because it changes the target less. I therefore calibrate every method to a target cross-entropy rise of 0.5 or 1 nat/token on validation text. I then evaluate the fixed edits on new European Parliament session text (Koehn 2005) to test whether their relative selectivity persists.

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
2 Methods

2.1 Model and data
The base model \(W_0\) is Goodfire’s four-layer, 67M-parameter decoder-only model, trained on a subset of the Pile and decomposed in the VPD report (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 3.1; Gao et al. 2020). Its 24 weight matrices comprise the query, key, value and output projections of attention and two MLP matrices per layer. The decomposition supplies 38,912 rank-one subcomponents, \(A_c = u_c v_c^\top\), which together form the VPD dictionary.
Europarl supplies one window per session date, starting at an aligned speaker turn so that languages share a common source context. Training windows serve selection and learning, and validation windows serve calibration. Evaluation uses 64 development dates and then 58 further dates, the confirmation set. I measure the change in mean next-token cross-entropy (CE) from \(W_0\), in nat/token. To check sensitivity to the chosen target-training subset, I repeat selection and training on three overlapping subsets, termed draws. Learned runs also use different seeds. The English retain pool combines Europarl, WikiText-2 (Merity et al. 2017) and English-filtered Pile text and is fixed across draws. Data sizes and implementation details are in Appendix A.


2.2 Subcomponent selection
An edit changes one weight matrix by \(W_m \leftarrow W_m + \alpha A_c\), leaving the other subcomponents and the decomposition residual fixed. The subcomponent is not normalized. In VPD each subcomponent has a scalar mask coefficient equal to 1 in the unedited model; the edit changes it to \(1 + \alpha\), and the edit norm is \(|\alpha|\,\lVert A_c\rVert_F\).
The selection rule ranks subcomponents by the target CE gradient relative to English Fisher curvature. The score favors target-CE increases with low predicted English KL for small coefficient changes: \[\frac{g_c^2}{q_c + \varepsilon \lVert A_c\rVert_F^2},\] where \(g_c\) is the derivative of target CE with respect to the mask coefficient, \(q_c\) is the directional Fisher estimate on the English retain pool, and \(\varepsilon\) supplies a small curvature floor. Because this score is local, the ranked shortlist is then tested at finite doses on target training text. The rule uses \(\alpha = \operatorname{sign}(g_c)\,a\), increasing the dose \(a\) up to 2. It accepts the first subcomponent to reach a target CE rise of 1 nat/token, falling back to the first that reaches 0.5 if none reaches 1. If neither threshold is reached, no edit is selected.


2.3 Comparison methods

Rank-one LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) learns both update vectors in layer 0’s attention output matrix, where all three selected subcomponents lie, matching their matrix and rank while learning its own direction.
Full-matrix fine-tuning allows learned changes across all 24 weight matrices.
Neuron edits select the top \(k\) MLP neurons by their excess activation frequency on target text over English, then reduce their output weights. Both \(k\) and the scale are calibrated to the target effect (Tang et al. 2024; Kojima et al. 2024).
Randomized-dictionary edits apply the subcomponent selection rule after independent random signed permutations of the dictionary’s input and output coordinates in each matrix. This preserves subcomponent norms and pairwise angles within each matrix while changing their alignment with the model’s weights. The control was planned to test whether disrupting this alignment changes selectivity under the same rule, provided matched edits could be found.

The learned updates are trained for 200 steps per draw, minimizing a per-window hinge penalty for target CE rises below 1 nat/token plus English KL divergence from \(W_0\), with weight 1. The final update is scaled to the required target effect.


2.4 Matching target effects
I calibrate every edit on target validation text to a CE rise of τ = 0.5 or 1 nat/token, within 0.02. Only these matched edits enter the comparison. For the main comparison, a prespecified tolerance of τ ± 0.1 nat/token applies to each edit’s mean target rise on evaluation text. I report the achieved target effects alongside related-language damage.
For each target, the selected subcomponent and calibrated doses were unchanged across the three draws, leaving six distinct edits across targets and effect sizes. All selected subcomponent edits use the negative direction, so their coefficient is \(1-a\): \(a=1\) removes the contribution and \(a>1\) reverses it. None is an exact ablation: three reduce the contribution without changing its sign and three reverse it, two only slightly (Table 1).


2.5 Evaluation
The related languages were excluded from this study’s selection and training inputs, but my earlier experiments had used their development text and identified the German subcomponent with Dutch in view. The edits, comparators and main analysis were fixed before the development readout on 64 session dates. The unchanged edits were then evaluated once on 58 further session dates, without recalibration. These new dates test the fixed edits on new text in the same languages, leaving the selection rule’s generalization untested. Appendix A.3 records the prior access and analysis chronology.

Edits were eligible only if no English evaluation set had a CE rise above 0.1 nat/token. I compare related-language CE rises using simultaneous 95% bootstrap intervals over session dates. These intervals condition on the selected edits and training runs. The analysis details are in Appendix A.2.

3 Results

3.1 Related-language damage
On the 58 new session dates, the six subcomponent edits raised related-language CE by 0.0003–0.0053 nat/token, compared with 0.027–0.876 across individual comparator runs (Figure 1; Table 2). All matched edits passed the English eligibility checks. Every edit in the main comparison also stayed within the prespecified target-effect tolerance.

All 18 mean differences between subcomponent edits and the three comparators have simultaneous 95% intervals below zero, with upper bounds at −0.023 nat/token or lower (Figure 2, top row; Appendix B). These comparisons reuse six subcomponent edits, each compared with three methods. The related-language advantage thus persists on text not used to calibrate the edits.

A separate post hoc analysis of related-language KL divergence from the base model gave the same ordering, with all 18 intervals below zero.

3.2 Achieved target effects
Staying within τ ± 0.1 still allows two methods’ target effects to differ, so a post hoc check compares them directly to assess whether the related-language advantage came with a smaller target effect. The simultaneous interval for the between-method target gap lies wholly within ±0.1 nat/token in 15 of 18 comparisons (Figure 2, bottom row). This agreement band was chosen after the results. The three remaining gaps occur at τ = 1 and have positive means: the subcomponent edit changes the target more on average, although one interval also permits a smaller effect. The observed advantage therefore does not appear to be driven by a weaker target effect. The subcomponent edits also had larger Frobenius weight-change norms than the learned updates (Table 2).

3.3 Preservation of English predictions
Passing the English CE limit does not imply equal preservation of English predictions. In a post hoc comparison of \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{W_0}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{edit}})\), LoRA had lower English KL than the subcomponent edits in 72/72 development comparisons and full-matrix fine-tuning in 65/72, across targets, draws, τ values and four English sets. On the single English set from the new dates, each learned method had lower KL in 18/18 comparisons across targets, draws and τ values (Table 2). These are dependent descriptive counts that reuse edits and text sets.
On the new dates, the subcomponent edits’ English KL was nevertheless below 10⁻³ nat/token. Both learned methods explicitly optimize English KL, whereas none of the methods optimizes retention of the related language.

3.4 Expanded training comparison
The main learned updates used 200 steps. Their selected learning rates lay at the edges of the tested grids (upper for LoRA, lower for full-matrix fine-tuning), so the grids may have missed better settings. To examine sensitivity to this recipe, an exploratory comparison used 2,000 steps, a larger hinge margin, wider learning-rate grids and more seeds, then calibrated the updates to the same τ. Evaluation used the previously evaluated development dates.
This expanded recipe reduced related-language damage for full-matrix fine-tuning in all six target and τ combinations and for LoRA in five, but the subcomponent edits retained their advantage. Achieved target effects differed from the subcomponent edits by at most 0.07 nat/token. Several training settings changed together, so the improvement cannot be attributed to step count alone. The training runs were not shown to converge at either budget, so the comparison does not establish the best selectivity these learned methods could attain. Appendix A.1 gives the extended comparison methods.


3.5 Choice within the VPD dictionary
Two alternative rules pick the subcomponent whose unit-norm direction has the largest absolute projection of a learned update. A third uses the target-minus-English difference in VPD’s learned scores for how much of each subcomponent to retain, termed causal importance (Appendix A.1). In these descriptive comparisons, all three rules caused at least as much related-language damage as the main selector wherever estimates were available. Some alternatives had no matched edit, and some comparisons used fewer draws. The causal-importance rule raised related-language CE by 0.48–1.37 nat/token more than the main selector on the new dates, at similar target effects. Reusing the previously chosen German subcomponent produced the same edit as the main selector. These comparisons show that the choice of direction matters for the tested edits.


3.6 Contribution of the dictionary
Testing what the dictionary contributes requires comparisons with directions outside it. The planned randomized-dictionary control produced no matched edit in any target–draw combination: no shortlisted subcomponent reached even 0.5 nat/token of target damage within the dose limit of 2. It therefore did not compare selectivity at the required target effect. Larger doses remain untested.
In exploratory comparisons, a whitened rank-one selector searched outside the dictionary using the target gradient and an approximate English Fisher curvature. Its calibrated edits caused more related-language damage than the VPD edits on development text. However, it used the selected VPD subcomponent’s norm and the main selector’s curvature floor, so this comparison does not isolate the dictionary’s contribution. Applying the main selector to singular components of the weight matrices yielded no eligible comparison: every edit that reached τ exceeded the English CE limit. These controls leave the dictionary’s contribution unresolved.

title: Selective Language Damage with Parameter-Decomposition Subcomponents
text:
4 Discussion
The methods rank differently for English and for the related languages. Learned updates better preserve English predictions, which their objective explicitly protects, while the selected VPD directions better spare the related languages absent from that objective. The comparison does not test learned updates trained to preserve the related language itself. Calibration also matches only the mean target effect. Because the learned objective penalizes each target window separately, equal means may hide different spreads of target damage across windows.
These conclusions concern six fixed edits in one small model, across three language pairs and two validation-calibrated target levels. They describe next-token prediction on parliamentary text.

Prior use of related-language development text and the earlier choice of the German subcomponent (Section 2.5), together with the inconclusive dictionary controls, limit what can be attributed to the selection procedure or decomposition. The dictionary’s contribution and the rule’s reliability on new tasks remain unresolved, and the study does not identify a language-specific mechanism. Within these limits, six fixed subcomponent edits in this model damaged the related languages less than rank-one LoRA, full-matrix fine-tuning and neuron edits calibrated to the same validation target effect, while the learned updates preserved English better.


Code and data. GitHub provides code, saved measurements and reproduction instructions. Analysis can be replayed from the per-date measurements; the confirmatory text and token windows are not released, preventing a rerun of that model evaluation from this checkout.

AI assistance. I used OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude for research planning, code development, data analysis and manuscript preparation. Scientific Agent Skills (Kassis et al. 2026) supplied the scientific-writing, scientific-critical-thinking, peer-review and citation-management workflows used to review organization, claims and references.

text:
Appendix A — Method details
Data. Europarl v7 (Koehn 2005) supplies one 257-token window per session date (256 predictions). Windows start at the same aligned speaker turn in each language, but each language is tokenized and truncated independently, so the windows need not cover identical content. Each target has three draws of 64 of its 128 training windows and 32 validation windows for calibration. The English validation set has 64 windows: 32 Europarl and 32 English-filtered Pile. The retain pool has 256 windows: 128 Europarl English training, 64 WikiText-2 validation and 64 English-filtered Pile validation.
Selection. The model Fisher estimate \(q_c\) averages squared directional scores using eight model-sampled label sets per retain window (Martens 2020; Kunstner et al. 2019). The floor \(\varepsilon\) is the 1st percentile of \(q_c / \lVert A_c\rVert_F^2\). The top 64 subcomponents are re-ranked using the larger of \(q_c\) and a second estimate on 256 other English windows, before the dose search of Section 2.2. Curvature checks passed on the NVIDIA L40S used for the original runs, but the batch-splitting check failed on the tested A10 and L4. Verified selector reruns cover only the German target’s first draw on the L40S, with the VPD dictionary and one randomized dictionary. GPU-dependent Fisher-label sampling can change selections on other hardware.
Calibration. The first dose-grid crossing of τ is bracketed, then bisected for at most five steps until within the matching tolerance. Neuron edits scale the top \(k\) neurons’ output weights by \(1-f\): calibration takes the smallest power-of-two \(k\) from 1 to 256 whose full removal reaches τ, then calibrates \(f\). Randomized dictionaries use a separate seed per draw.
Learned updates. The 200-step updates use Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015), 10 warm-up steps, gradient clipping at 1.0, and 8 target and 8 English windows per step. Calibration scales the final update \(D\) to \(\beta D\), with \(\beta \le 1\). The learning rate is chosen once per target on draw 0, by the lowest English validation KL at τ = 1. Every target chose 3e-3 for LoRA and 1e-6 for full-matrix fine-tuning, respectively the upper and lower edges of the tested grids.

A.1 Alternative selectors and extended training
Two within-dictionary alternatives use the first step of orthogonal matching pursuit (Pati et al. 1993; Mallat and Zhang 1993): they normalize each subcomponent to unit Frobenius norm, select the one with the largest absolute inner product with a learned update, and use that inner product’s sign. One uses full-matrix fine-tuning; the other uses rank-one LoRA across all 24 matrices. VPD’s learned causal-importance score sets the lower bound on a subcomponent’s mask during decomposition training. A third rule selects the largest mean target-minus-English score with a negative sign, adapting Bushnaq’s top-16 ranking to one subcomponent (Bushnaq 2026). The fourth alternative reuses the previously chosen German subcomponent. All use the main calibration rule. Some fail to reach τ or lack an eligible learned checkpoint; their contrasts include only the available matched, usable draws and use a separate simultaneous family.
The extended learned updates use 2,000 steps, a hinge margin of 1.5, wider learning-rate grids and three seeds per draw. The whitened selector maximizes the squared target gradient relative to damped K-FAC curvature on English text (Martens and Grosse 2015), then tests doses from 1/64 to 8. The SVD control applies the main selection rule unchanged to the singular components of all 24 weight matrices; these reconstruct the weights exactly, whereas VPD leaves a residual.
Extended contrasts compare unpaired means over each method’s matched, usable runs. A sensitivity analysis excludes 7 of 27 LoRA runs whose English validation KL at step 2,000 exceeded twice their minimum from step 100 onward. Both analyses favour the subcomponent edits. Training diagnostics did not establish objective convergence and were not used to select edits.
These exploratory comparisons were specified before the runs. Analysis rules were fixed before readout, after selection outcomes and target and English validation effects were known. This chronology comes from the author’s records, without independent timestamps.


A.2 Evaluation and intervals
Evaluation sets. Development uses 64 session dates. English eligibility checks use Europarl test text (64 windows), WikiText-2 test text (32) and Pile test documents (512). Confirmation uses 58 further dates (48 main and 10 reserve, analysed together), including English. An edit must pass both development and confirmatory English checks to enter a confirmatory comparison.
Main comparisons. The planned family contains four comparators × three language pairs × two values of τ. Each contrast is the subcomponent edit’s CE rise minus the comparator’s, averaged over matched, eligible draws and then over dates. Simultaneous 95% intervals use 2,000 shared bootstrap resamples of session dates (Efron 1979) and a max-|t| critical value (Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller 2019, supplement, Algorithm 3). Training draws and seeds, selected subcomponents, language pairs and the model remain fixed. The randomized-dictionary contrasts have no estimates because the control produced no feasible edits.
Target-effect checks. The prespecified tolerance for each edit’s target CE rise was τ ± 0.1 nat/token; all edits in the main confirmation comparison met it. The post hoc agreement analysis instead compares the target effects of two methods. Its simultaneous family includes 54 coordinates per readout: target gaps, related-language CE contrasts and related-language KL contrasts, using 20,000 shared date resamples. KL is \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{W_0}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{edit}})\), averaged over next-token positions.


A.3 Prior data access
The selection, comparison and analysis rules were fixed on 11 October 2026 before the development readout. Later that day, the unchanged edits were evaluated once on 58 further dates under an amendment fixed before those windows were parsed. The chronology relies on the author’s records; there is no independently timestamped preregistration.
In an earlier experiment, I had chosen German subcomponent 0.attn.o:268 with Dutch in view. It was also the top German candidate in a pilot of this selector. Dutch, Portuguese and Italian development text and NTREX Dutch and Italian text (Federmann et al. 2022) had been read or used previously. The development dates therefore do not provide a fresh test. The Pile also contains a European Parliament component (Gao et al. 2020, sec. 2.17); overlap with the model’s pretraining subset is unknown.

1 Introduction
A repair is an additional weight update trained to reduce fine-tuning’s collateral damage while preserving its intended effect. When a recipe is repeated on new samples, a repair learned for an earlier fine-tune, the donor, may help repair the next one. Reusing its fixed directions trains only 24 coefficients per target; using it as an initialization allows the repair directions to change.
I test these alternatives by deliberately worsening German next-token prediction, which also raises Dutch cross-entropy (CE), a measure of prediction loss. Dutch is excluded from the fine-tuning objective. In this controlled test, repair must restore Dutch prediction while preserving the German change. The donor and two target fine-tunes are trained independently from one base model, with the same recipe but different seeds and training dates from the same Europarl distribution (Koehn 2005). I use Goodfire’s model from its adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) study (Bushnaq et al. 2026, sec. 3.1). Repairs act on its weights without using the decomposition. Scalar refitting has the same fixed-direction form as coefficient edits of a decomposition (Section 4).
Task arithmetic adds or subtracts a weight difference with a single scale (Ilharco et al. 2023). RESTA reuses a safety vector with a fixed global scale in its main experiments (Bhardwaj et al. 2024), while SafeGene learns a scalar per selected layer for frozen distilled safety adapters (Wang et al. 2026, sec. 3.5 and 4.4). SPoT instead uses learned source-task soft prompts to initialize target-task training (Vu et al. 2022). Here I compare fixed-direction reuse and donor initialization at matched rank on the same targets. Fresh and random starts test the value of donor initialization, and Section 3.3 compares fitting costs.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
2 Setup
Model and fine-tunes. The base is a four-layer, 67M-parameter decoder-only model pretrained on a subset of the Pile (Gao et al. 2020). Each fine-tune adds \(D\) to the 24 attention and MLP matrices. A hinge term raises German CE while KL keeps English, French, Spanish and Italian, the retain languages, close to the base model. Both targets raise Dutch CE by about 0.19 nat/token on held-out evaluation text (method details).
Repair objective and recovery. Each repair adds a rank-one update \(E_m=b_m a_m^{\top}\) to each of the 24 matrices, with input factor \(a_m\) and output factor \(b_m\). All repairs obey the same norm cap, \(\lVert E\rVert_F\le\lVert D\rVert_F\), where the norms cover all 24 matrices. The loss sums three equally weighted mean KL divergences \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\text{teacher}}\,\|\,p_{\text{repair}})\): to the base model on Dutch positions, rewarding restoration of Dutch predictions, and to the fine-tuned model on German and retain positions, penalizing reversal of the German effect or changes to retain predictions. Recovery measures the share of Dutch CE damage removed by repair \(X\): \[r_{\text{nl}}(X) = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(X) - \mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(\text{base})}{\mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(\text{fine-tuned}) - \mathrm{CE}_{\text{nl}}(\text{base})}.\] Recovery differences are in percentage points (pp).
Families. One donor repair, learned from fresh initialization on 73,728 prediction positions, serves both targets. Scalar-only fitting learns coefficients in \(E_m=c_m b_m a_m^{\top}\) over its fixed factors. Other families train one or both factors (Table 1). Applying the capped donor repair without target fitting gives the fixed donor repair reference.

The first fresh seed uses the random input vectors from which the donor repair was trained. Its comparison with donor initialization assesses donor training as a whole, without isolating directions, norm or checkpoint selection. The second fresh seed uses an independent draw. Second seeds of fresh and random initialization were tested only at 2,048 fit tokens with a 600-step cap.
Budgets and step caps. A fit budget counts the unique prediction positions (fit tokens) used for fitting: 256, 512 or 2,048, nested so that larger budgets add text to smaller ones. They exclude a shared selection and diagnostic pool of 57,344 positions. All families and both targets share fitting, selection and evaluation windows. Ordinary fitting runs full-batch Adam at four learning rates per family, with a 10-step warm-up and then a constant rate, saving a checkpoint every 50 steps. A step cap of 50, 100, 200 or 600 limits selection to checkpoints saved up to that step, so the chosen checkpoint can precede the cap (fitting details). The full budget is 2,048 fit tokens with a 600-step cap for ordinary runs.
Selection and readout. Evaluation text is grouped by Europarl session date, with one 256-prediction window per language per date. For each family, budget and cap, selection on 32 dates separate from fitting favors Dutch recovery among candidates preserving the German effect and reducing Dutch KL from the base, with a guard on retain-language CE (full rule). Selected repairs are evaluated once on 92 other validation-period dates, the readout, separate from earlier project windows. The readout constraints recheck German-effect preservation, positive Dutch KL recovery and retain-language CE drift there (thresholds in Table 6). Within each fixed target, one joint date bootstrap (Efron 1979) gives paired 95% percentile intervals.
Primary comparison. Donor initialization is compared with scalar-only fitting at the full budget. To check whether the 600-step cap stops scalar fitting too early, the expanded scalar search adds two projected-gradient runs on the same loss from two starts, so optimization budgets are unequal. Selection pools their final candidates with the 48 ordinary checkpoints (details).
An advantage above 3 pp is established when the whole paired interval exceeds 3 pp, excluded when wholly below, and undecided otherwise. Interpretation requires measurable Dutch damage, both selected repairs meeting the readout constraints, and both additional scalar runs meeting the declared stopping criteria (Table 6; checks). Other contrasts are descriptive, without multiplicity correction. Their intervals determine whether the sign is positive, negative or undecided. Five contrasts in Table 3 also assess equivalence within ±2 pp. The protocol fixed both margins without a stated derivation.

3 Results

3.1 Fixed directions fall short
Without target fitting, the capped donor repair recovers 86.3% and 58.6% of Dutch damage on the primary and replication targets. At 2,048 fit tokens, the expanded scalar search raises recovery to 86.9% and 78.4%, while training both factors from the donor start reaches 98.2% and 98.8% (Figure 1).
Both additional scalar runs on each target met the declared stopping criteria (Table 7). They left selection unchanged on the primary target and raised replication recovery from 77.3% to 78.4% (Table 6).
Both targets meet the conditions for interpreting the primary contrast (Table 6 and Table 7). Donor initialization exceeds the expanded scalar search by 11.3 pp [+10.0, +12.7] on the primary target (Table 2) and 20.4 pp [+19.0, +21.7] on the replication target. Both intervals lie entirely above the prespecified 3 pp margin.
The scalar shortfall is already present on the fitting data, so it is not confined to new text. At the full budget, the selected scalar repairs remove 87.0% and 79.2% of the fine-tune’s Dutch KL from the base model, against at least 98.4% for every factor-training family. This measures KL recovery, whereas readout uses CE. The bounded search cannot distinguish limitations of the fixed directions under the norm cap from remaining optimization error.
At the full budget, training only the output vectors from the donor start closes most of the gap: output-only fitting recovers 10.2 and 19.1 pp more than the expanded scalar search on the primary and replication targets, and training both factors adds 1.1 and 1.3 pp (Table 3). Without a frozen-random-input control, the benefit of the donor’s learned input vectors remains unresolved.

3.3 What donor initialization saves
Each combination of family, fit budget and step cap is a cell. The reference is the first fresh seed at the full budget. A cell reaches it if the selected repair satisfies the readout constraints and the lower bound of its paired 95% interval for recovery minus reference recovery is strictly above −2 pp. Presentations count fit tokens × optimizer steps over all four learning-rate runs. The cheapest reaching donor and fresh cells use 256 and 2,048 tokens, respectively, with 50-step caps: 51,200 versus 409,600 presentations, one eighth as many. Fresh fitting also reaches with 256 tokens at a 600-step cap, so both families have the same minimum of 256 unique fit tokens, or 57,600 with the shared 57,344 selection positions. This saves presentations without reducing the unique-token requirement.
Training the donor repair took 3,686,400 presentations, so this per-target difference would repay its cost from the eleventh target, a projection from two tested targets. The estimated GPU-time saving is much smaller (Table 4), moving break-even to about 151 and 106 targets for the primary and replication targets, without establishing an end-to-end time saving. Checkpoints are selected before readout, but the cheapest reaching cells were chosen afterward, and the intervals describe cells, not the cost ratio. These estimates depend on the reference seed, the one-sided reach threshold and the tested grid (cost accounting).

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
4 Discussion
Rescaling the donor’s fixed directions recovered 86.9% and 78.4% of Dutch damage after target fitting. Training the rank-one factors recovered at least 95.6% across the tested starts and fit budgets with a 600-step cap. The donor start added little over fresh fitting at the full budget, but helped more in the tested short runs: its cheapest reaching cell used one eighth of fresh fitting’s token presentations. The two families had the same minimum unique fit-token budget. In this setting, the donor repair was more useful as a starting point than as a set of fixed directions.
The scalar shortfall is already visible on the scalar fits’ own fitting data. Coefficient edits of a parameter decomposition such as VPD (Bushnaq et al. 2026) also rescale fixed rank-one components. As an interpretation not tested here, fitting such coefficients on the edit’s own data could flag a shortfall before evaluation on new text, although it would not distinguish limitations of the components from optimization error under a given search and norm cap.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
5 Limits of these conclusions
These results concern one donor, one recipe and one model, with two targets analysed separately. Date-bootstrap intervals cover variation across readout dates for fixed repairs, not across fine-tunes, donors, recipes or fitting windows. Second seeds were tested only at the full budget, leaving short-run results conditional on the tested starts and shared fitting windows. I do not analyse what the repair directions represent or how they restore Dutch prediction. Without an output-only control with frozen random input vectors, the donor input vectors’ contribution is also unresolved; Zhu et al. (2024) studied such frozen random inputs. The study does not test new-skill transfer or safety alignment, including the safety settings of RESTA and SafeGene.
AI assistance. I used OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude for research planning, code development, data analysis and manuscript preparation. Scientific Agent Skills (Kassis et al. 2026) supplied the scientific-writing, scientific-critical-thinking, peer-review and citation-management workflows used to review organization, claims and references.

Appendix A — Method details
Fine-tunes. Adam (Kingma and Ba 2015) learns full-matrix additive updates \(D_m\) to each layer’s query, key, value, output and two MLP matrices (24 total), with embeddings and norms frozen. It runs at learning rate 3e-6 for 200 steps on the per-window hinge \(\max(0, 1 - \Delta\mathrm{CE}_{\text{de}})\) (1-nat margin) plus retain-language KL with weight 1. German validation dates determine the checkpoint.
Repairs. Ordinary fitting uses Adam. The donor starts fresh (Table 1), using 73,728 prediction positions, three learning rates and 200 minibatch steps per run. Checkpoints saved every 25 steps undergo selection on donor validation windows by the rule below. Targets save checkpoints every 50 steps at four learning rates (Table 5): 48 candidates per family at the 600-step cap. Donor starts are capped as \(\min(1, \lVert D\rVert_F / \lVert E_{\text{donor}}\rVert_F)\, E_{\text{donor}}\).

The 50-step cap uses the same grid. Several output-only cells and donor-initialized replication at 512 tokens select the first checkpoint at the lowest rate, which can explain repeated values across caps. Advantages over fresh and random starts are nonmonotonic in budget and cap.
Selection. Feasibility requires a German-damage ratio (with repair / without repair) of 0.9–1.1, German KL drift from the fine-tune at most 0.05 times the base model’s KL from it, and Dutch movement toward the base. Feasible candidates rank by Dutch recovery, then smaller norm, then listing order. Of the top five, selection takes the first raising no retain language’s CE by more than 0.01 nat/token.
Data. Fit budgets exclude each window’s initial context token and split predictions 2:1:1 across Dutch, German and retain text. At 256 tokens, one Dutch window contributes 128 predictions, one German 64, and four retain windows 16 each. At 512 tokens these counts double. At 2,048, four Dutch and two German windows contribute 256 each, and one per retain language contributes 128. Target fit windows and selection dates are separate from the donor’s.
Selection and readout use 32 and 92 dates, respectively, with one 257-token window (256 predictions) per language from the same turn. Portuguese, the seventh language, is diagnostic only: its selection windows count toward token and evaluation costs, but not the loss or selection constraints. Readout dates were ineligible if present in recorded project data, pilot or run files, or if their windows duplicated text in use. All passed. Prior model exposure remains unresolved.
Assessability. The primary contrast requires a Dutch-damage readout interval with lower bound at least 0.025 nat/token. Damage is 0.187 nat/token [0.178, 0.196] on the primary target and 0.189 [0.180, 0.198] on replication. Both selected repairs must satisfy the readout constraints (Table 6), and both additional scalar runs must meet the stopping criteria.
Study record. My records place a dated protocol fixing rules, margins and families before readout-data construction and target fine-tuning. An author-dated amendment fixed readout data and clarified the primary interpretation before any target fine-tune or readout, without changing decision rules. The unpublished protocol, amendment and log lack independent timestamps. This is not verifiable preregistration.
Uncertainty. Within each target, 5,000 joint date resamples cover all budgets and caps, computing recovery ratios from mean damages. Readout constraints use point estimates over all dates. Equivalence is assessed only for the five contrasts marked in Table 3. It remains unestablished between donor and random initialization at every budget and cap.

It combines the spectral step of Barzilai and Borwein (1988), the projected-gradient scheme of Birgin et al. The declared stopping criteria require finite values for all losses and gradients, including line-search trials, initial training/export loss agreement within 1e-5 nat/token, and at least one stopping condition: projected-gradient norm at most 1e-4 of its reference; relative fit-loss decrease below 1e-7 for five iterations; or the line-search floor with stationarity at most 1e-3 of that reference. Both starts use the initial coefficients’ projected-gradient reference. Final-loss agreement is descriptive, not a stopping criterion.

title: Transferring Learned Repairs Between Fine-Tunes
text:
Appendix C — Cost accounting
For each cost measure, let \(C^*\) be a family’s cheapest reaching cost on the tested grid. If the observed per-target difference repeats, reuse repays the donor cost after more than \[
K^* = \frac{C_{\text{donor}}}{C^*(\text{fresh}) - C^*(\text{donor initialization})}
\] targets (Table 4). The donor’s 3,686,400 presentations give \(K^* \approx 10.3\): an 11-target projection from two targets. Neither scalar-only fitting nor the fixed donor repair reaches the reference (Figure 3). A random start saves no presentations on the primary target. On replication it gives \(K^* = 18\), charged with the full donor cost despite using only the donor repair’s norm.
Unique tokens count fit tokens plus 57,344 selection positions (32 dates × 7 languages × 256). Presentations count fit tokens × optimizer steps across all four learning rates up to the cap, excluding selection forward passes. GPU seconds combine training time prorated to the cap and selection-evaluation time allocated by candidate count. For the expanded scalar search, presentations and GPU seconds also include both additional runs and evaluation of the 48 checkpoints used to choose the second start. All cells exclude base/fine-tuned readouts, the pre-fitting damage check and exploration of other cells.
The donor costs 131,072 unique tokens (73,728 fit plus selection), 3,686,400 presentations (3 learning rates × 200 steps × 6,144 tokens per minibatch), and an estimated 336 GPU seconds for training, selection and readout. Its fine-tune is excluded because the donor model is assumed to exist.
The first fresh seed is the reference (Section 3.3), with self-comparison interval [0, 0]. At 256 tokens and a 600-step cap, fresh fitting’s lower bounds, −1.985 pp (primary) and −1.957 pp (replication), narrowly exceed −2 pp and set its lowest unique-token cost. Sensitivity to another reference seed remains unevaluated.

title: Some Studies of Language Model Weight Edits
text:
Some Studies of Language Model Weight Edits
The work presented here is my attempt to understand interpretability and model editing methods more deeply. By building on recent advances and trying to find something new, I also learn what others have done before me. For me, the best way to learn is through practice.
Although these studies are written in the form of research papers, I’m not yet confident that I can call them rigorous scientific work. I’m sharing them in the hope that they may be useful to someone besides me.

AI assistance
I made extensive use of Codex with GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, as well as Claude Code with Opus 5.5, throughout this work. I personally supervised the experiments and guided their direction based on the results and the questions I wanted to explore.
Most of the text was also written with AI assistance and went through several rounds of careful editing. I hope attentive readers will forgive me for that.





Selective language editing
To test selectivity, I deliberately weaken predictions in one language and measure damage to a close relative, following up on Lucius Bushnaq’s exploration of fine-tuning with parameter decomposition. Across three related-language pairs, selected subcomponent edits caused less damage to the related language than rank-one LoRA, full-matrix fine-tuning and neuron edits calibrated to the same target effect on validation text. LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning preserved English predictions better.

Repair transfer
In these experiments, fine-tuning a model to worsen German predictions also damages Dutch predictions. A repair is an added weight update trained to reduce the Dutch damage while keeping the intended German change. I compare ways to reuse an earlier repair on two fine-tunes trained independently from the same base model on samples from the same data distribution. Fitting only scalar coefficients over the repair's fixed directions left more Dutch damage than training the directions. Starting from the earlier repair removed more Dutch damage than fitting a new repair when data and steps were limited. With the most data and steps tested, a new repair nearly caught up.

title: Repair transfer

Training the repair
The earlier fine-tune is the donor and its correction is the donor repair. The primary target is the first new fine-tuned model I repair. I repeat the comparison on a second model, the replication target. All three models are fine-tuned separately from the same base model, using the same recipe with different seeds and samples from the same distribution of European Parliament text (Europarl).
To learn a repair, I freeze the fine-tuned weights and train an added update to restore the base model’s Dutch predictions while preserving the fine-tuned model’s predictions in the other languages. I learn the donor repair once, then reuse it for both targets.
Each repair adds a rank-one update, formed from an input and an output vector, to each of 24 weight matrices. I compare three ways to train the repair:

Scalar coefficients only: keep the donor’s vectors fixed and learn one scalar coefficient per matrix, separately for each target.
Donor initialization: start from the donor’s vectors and train both on the new fine-tune.
Fresh initialization: learn both vectors from scratch, without using the donor repair.

title: Selective language editing
text:
Edit one rank-one subcomponent
To make a targeted weight change, I select one subcomponent from Goodfire’s adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) and adjust its contribution. VPD writes a weight matrix \(W\) as a sum of rank-one subcomponents plus a residual. The decomposition is trained so that few subcomponents are needed on any input. Each subcomponent \(A\) is the outer product of an output vector \(u_{\mathrm{out}}\) and an input vector \(v_{\mathrm{in}}\):
\[
A = u_{\mathrm{out}}v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top.
\]
For an input \(x\), the input vector reads out one number, \(v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x\). The output vector determines the direction in which that number contributes to the matrix’s output:
\[
Ax = u_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(v_{\mathrm{in}}^\top x\bigr).
\]
A fixed rule uses target-language and English text to favor subcomponents expected to weaken the target language while changing English predictions little.
The edit changes a single number, the selected subcomponent’s coefficient \(c\):
\[
W_{\mathrm{edited}} = (W-A) + cA.
\]
Changing this coefficient changes many entries of the weight matrix. The subcomponent’s two vectors stay fixed, as do all other subcomponents and the residual. At \(c=1\) the matrix is unchanged. Setting \(c=0\) removes the selected contribution, and \(c<0\) reverses its sign. The slider below illustrates this operation on a toy matrix.

title: Selective language editing
section: Comparing ways to change the weights
text:
Comparing ways to change the weights
I compare the VPD edit with three other ways to change the weights, all aimed at worsening target-language prediction while preserving English predictions.
Rank-one LoRA learns its own output and input vectors in the same weight matrix:
\[
\Delta W_{\mathrm{LoRA}} = a_{\mathrm{out}}b_{\mathrm{in}}^\top.
\]
This lets LoRA choose a different direction while keeping the update’s rank and the edited matrix fixed.
Full-matrix fine-tuning gives the learned update more freedom: it can change every entry in the model’s 24 attention and feed-forward weight matrices.
The neuron edit selects neurons by how much more often they activate on target text than on English text, then scales their output weights.
LoRA and full-matrix fine-tuning penalize changes to the original model’s English predictions during training. These selection and training steps use no Dutch, Portuguese or Italian text. Those languages test whether the methods also spare a close relative that they were not explicitly trained to preserve.

title: Selective language editing
text:
Matching the intended damage
To compare side effects fairly, I first make each method worsen the target language by a similar amount. Otherwise, a method might spare Dutch simply because it barely changed German.
I calibrate each edit by adjusting its strength on target-language validation text. I use two calibration levels: an increase of 0.5 or 1 nat/token in average prediction loss (cross-entropy) relative to the original model.
I use Europarl v7, a corpus of European Parliament proceedings. After calibration, I measure the damage to both languages on separate text from 58 session dates.
